fixes.explanation: You got it, baker! The verse says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." No spot is left out, not even a quiet corner. The verse puts no limit on where. And what He observes is both the evil and the good.

The temple is a fine place to think of, but the verse doesn't draw a fence like that. It says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." Every place is a BIG list, friend. That leaves nothing out.

Jerusalem is one specific place, but the verse doesn't name any city at all. It says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." That covers Jerusalem and everything outside it too.

Guarding sounds nice, but it isn't in this verse. Here the perverse tongue doesn't protect anybody's spirit, it crushes it. Picture a cookie under a rolling pin that's way too heavy. That's crumbs, not protection, and the verse says "…a perverse tongue crushes the spirit."

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight." Notice it sets a sacrifice next to a prayer, and the LORD's reaction splits them: detestable on one side, His delight on the other. That's about as far apart as two reactions can get. Detestable is a strong word, and it's the one the verse picks.

Right, friend. The verse says, "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD—how much more the hearts of men!" Those two lie open before Him. So the "…how much more…" tells you hearts are no harder for Him to see. Nothing in there is hidden from Him.

That's it, baker. The verse says, "Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred." A fattened ox is a fancy meal, and it still loses to a plain dish with love at the table. The verse calls the dish of vegetables where there is love the better one.

Right, baker. The verse says, "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger calms dispute." One person adds fuel and the other takes it away. The verse puts them side by side, and the results go opposite ways. Being slow to anger is quiet work, but it does calm things down.
Grief isn't the word in this verse, friend. It says, "Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment…" The one lacking judgment finds joy in it. Meanwhile the man of understanding walks a straight path.
Shame isn't the word the verse uses, friend. It says, "Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment…" He enjoys it. The man of understanding is the one walking the straight path.

Yes, baker! The verse says, "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed." It puts failure on the side of lacking counsel and success on the side of many advisers. So the verse points you toward asking around. One more voice in the kitchen never hurt a batch.
That's the first half of the verse, friend. "Plans fail for lack of counsel…" is where that comes from. The second half gives the other result: "…with many advisers they succeed."

Backward is a fun guess, friend, but the verse picks a different direction. It says, "The path of life leads upward for the wise…" Then it mentions going down to Sheol. So the picture is up against down.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow." A widow is a woman whose husband has died. The verse says it's her boundaries He protects. The proud get their house torn down, and she gets her boundaries protected.
A king is a fair guess, friend, but the verse names someone else. It says, "The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow." The one named is the widow.

Hold on, baker, the verse reaches wider than that. It says, "He who is greedy for unjust gain brings trouble on his household…" The trouble lands on the whole house, not just the one chasing the money. So the verse doesn't leave the household out of it.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked blurts out evil." The righteous heart does its thinking first. That's the opposite of blurting.

Staying silent is a different thing from what the verse describes. It says, "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer…" The heart is pondering how to answer, not going quiet. The wicked mouth blurts, and the righteous heart thinks.

That's right, baker. The verse says, "The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous." That's a heavy line, and the verse doesn't soften it. Then it turns on a dime to the prayer of the righteous. I'd rather be on the hearing side of that verse.

Close to isn't what the verse says, friend. It says, "The LORD is far from the wicked…" So close to flips the first half around. The word for the righteous is hears: "…He hears the prayer of the righteous."

Right, friend. The verse says, "He who ignores discipline despises himself, but whoever heeds correction gains understanding." Ignoring discipline doesn't protect him. The verse puts the two side by side. The one who heeds correction gains understanding.

Yes, baker! The chapter closes with "The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor." Humility is named first and honor comes after it. Honor doesn't get to cut the line. That's the order the verse sets.
Wealth isn't in this last line, friend. It says, "…humility comes before honor." Wealth gets no spot in that sentence. The chapter ends with humility going first.
